Paragraph: While Lakshmana was suspecting Bharata of treachery and Rama was allaying those suspicions, Bharata was organizing his men. He bade Guha, to take a thousand of his relatives, well armed to carry on the search. He would walk with his Gurus, his people his ministers and citizens and Satrughna was to lead the search with the hill people. Unable to endure Rama's absence any longer Bharata burst out saying "Peace eludes me and so long as my brother and Sita are not found, so long will my anguish continue. The unrest that rages in me will be quelled the day Rama is crowned king of Kosala. Blessed is Lakshmana who always beholds Rama and blessed is Sita, as she ever follows that lord of the earth. As Kubera brings splendor to the Nandanavana so does Rama to Chitrakuta. Striding hurriedly through clumps of trees following the wisps of smoke, Bharata felt the thrill of a drowning man reaching the shores of mighty ocean.
Situation/Problem_Faced: Bharata is consumed by an intense sense of anguish and unrest due to Rama's absence. Despite his active organization of the search, his emotional state remains deeply distressed until Rama is found and restored to his rightful place.
Key_Teaching/Action_Taken: Bharata manages his overwhelming grief and anxiety by channelizing his energy into decisive action: organizing a widespread search for Rama. His passionate outburst, articulating that 'Peace eludes me' and 'my anguish will continue' until Rama is crowned, underscores the depth of his emotional suffering. He expresses admiration for Lakshmana and Sita for their constant proximity to Rama, highlighting his own feeling of deprivation. The 'thrill of a drowning man reaching the shores' vividly describes his desperate hope and the psychological relief that comes with even a hint of success.
Outcome/Resolution: Bharata's active organization of the search, fueled by his deep anguish, directs his efforts towards finding Rama. The sighting of smoke and the subsequent 'thrill' indicate a moment of profound hope and a potential alleviation of his intense suffering, marking a shift from despair to a sense of imminent resolution.

Spiritual_Psychological_Concept_Indian.Concept: Viraha (Separation-induced grief: Bharata's 'anguish' and 'unrest' due to Rama's absence are clear manifestations of Viraha.)
Dharma (Righteous duty: Bharata's unwavering resolve to restore Rama to the throne, despite his own suffering, is driven by his commitment to Dharma.)
Utsaha (Enthusiasm/Zeal: Despite his inner turmoil, Bharata displays immense Utsaha in his relentless search for Rama.)

Chitta Vritti Nirodha (Cessation of mind-fluctuations: Bharata's statement that his 'unrest...will be quelled the day Rama is crowned' implies that his mental fluctuations will only cease with the fulfillment of his righteous goal.)

Brief_Summary_Spiritual: The passage illustrates Bharata's intense Viraha (separation-induced grief), which manifests as deep 'anguish' and 'unrest'. Despite this, his actions are guided by unwavering Dharma (righteous duty) to restore Rama. His relentless search, driven by a profound Utsaha (zeal), underscores his spiritual commitment. The hope of finding Rama offers a glimpse of Chitta Vritti Nirodha, where his turbulent mind may finally find peace upon fulfilling his sacred purpose.
Brief_Summary_Psychological: Psychologically, Bharata is in a state of profound grief and anxiety stemming from Rama's absence, manifesting as a pervasive 'unrest'. He actively engages in stress management by meticulously organizing a search, channeling his emotional energy into purposeful action. His poignant outburst reveals the depth of his 'anguish', emphasizing that his psychological peace is entirely dependent on Rama's return to the throne. The 'thrill of a drowning man' vividly captures the intense hope and anticipation that comes with the prospect of finding relief from prolonged emotional suffering.
